families.s: HSE agricultural workplace-transport and farm-vehicle guidance
families.t: vehicle selection, routes, pedestrian separation, visibility, maintenance, parking, loading and operator competence
f: Farm transport activities should be broken into vehicle, driver and site factors so risks can be identified and controlled.
Vehicles, machines and handling equipment should be suitable for the work and maintained in safe condition.
Traffic routes should be planned to reduce conflict between vehicles, pedestrians, animals and buildings.
Operators need instruction, training and competence for the vehicle and tasks they perform.
Safe access to and exit from vehicles should be provided and used.
ATVs and other farm vehicles require controls matched to terrain, slope, load and operator capability.
Parking, loading, unloading, hitching and reversing arrangements should be included in the transport assessment.
Visibility, lighting, speed, route condition and visiting drivers should be managed rather than left to individual judgement.
families.g: Farm-transport risk depends on vehicle type, route geometry, terrain, weather, load, pedestrians, livestock, maintenance, visibility and operator competence.

families.s: HSE agricultural-machinery guarding, Safe Stop and maintenance guidance
families.t: dangerous parts, guards, Safe Stop, isolation, blockage clearance, attachments, test runs, maintenance and training
f: Agricultural machinery can expose workers to augers, cutters, intake mechanisms, belts, chains and other dangerous moving parts.
Guards and protective devices should be correctly fitted, effective and maintained in good condition.
Safe Stop should be applied before leaving the operating position or approaching dangerous parts.
Blocked, jammed or damaged machinery should be isolated before intervention.
Machines and attachments should be securely connected and compatible with the towing or power unit.
A test run does not remove the need to repeat isolation before further checking or adjustment.
Risk assessment should cover normal work, cleaning, maintenance, foreseeable misuse and young or inexperienced workers.
Repairs should be planned, supported safely and carried out by people with suitable competence and equipment.
families.g: Machinery risk depends on machine design, guarding, energy sources, task, blockage, attachment, maintenance, operator position, supervision and production pressure.

families.s: HSE power-take-off and PTO-drive-shaft guarding guidance
families.t: master shields, shaft guards, restraint chains, compatibility, inspection, shutdown, storage and entanglement prevention
f: Tractor PTOs and PTO drive shafts are very dangerous when not correctly guarded.
The tractor master shield and the complete rotating shaft should be protected by effective guards.
The shaft guard should rotate freely and its restraint chain should prevent the guard itself from rotating.
Guards should be checked before use and damaged or missing parts replaced.
Loose clothing, hair and materials can become entangled in exposed rotating shafts.
Power should be disengaged, the engine stopped and movement ceased before approaching or working on the shaft.
Shaft length, guard overlap and connection should be compatible with the tractor and machine throughout movement.
Stored machines should protect PTO guards from damage by weather, vehicles or livestock.
families.g: PTO risk depends on guard completeness, shaft speed, compatibility, restraint, clothing, access, shutdown, maintenance and the position of other people.

families.s: HSE ATV, quad-bike and side-by-side-vehicle safety guidance
families.t: training, active riding, terrain, helmets, passenger restrictions, loads, towing, maintenance and route assessment
f: Quad-bike and ATV operators need appropriate training for the machine and tasks required.
Sit-astride ATVs require active riding so the operator can shift body weight for terrain and slope conditions.
A suitable helmet should be worn where the assessment requires head protection.
Passengers should not be carried unless the vehicle is specifically designed for them.
Loads and towed equipment should remain within the manufacturer's limits and be secured.
Terrain, slopes, ditches, surfaces and route edges should be assessed before use.
Machine checks and maintenance should cover tyres, brakes, steering, controls and safety equipment.
Speed and route choice should allow the operator to remain in control under foreseeable ground and weather conditions.
families.g: ATV risk depends on vehicle type, terrain, slope, speed, load, passenger use, helmet, training, maintenance and operator fitness.

families.s: HSE adult-cattle handling, housing and public-risk guidance
families.t: handling systems, races, crushes, gates, bulls, animal behaviour, worker competence, escape and public access
f: Adult cattle should be handled using suitable races, pens, gates and a properly designed crush.
The handling system should restrain animals without exposing people to crushing or kicking.
People handling cattle need competence in animal behaviour and in using the equipment provided.
Curved races and solid-sided forcing areas can improve cattle flow and reduce risky manual intervention.
Stock bulls and bull beef require specific housing and handling precautions.
Workers should have a safe escape route and should not enter unsafe spaces with unsecured animals.
Animal health, temperament, familiarity with handling and the presence of calves affect behaviour and risk.
Public-access risks require separate assessment where cattle are kept in fields crossed by rights of way.
families.g: Cattle risk depends on animal class and behaviour, handling-system design, worker competence, escape routes, staffing, housing, public access and task timing.

families.s: HSE slurry-store, mixing, toxic-gas and drowning guidance
families.t: hydrogen sulphide, agitation, ventilation, exclusion, rescue, storage security, machinery and confined-space controls
f: Slurry stores, pits, tanks and chambers can contain dangerous atmospheres and present drowning risks.
Slurry gases can be present in slatted cattle housing and poorly ventilated areas as well as enclosed spaces.
Managing slurry requires controls for storage, mixing, pumping, access and machinery.
People should be excluded from dangerous areas during agitation and until gases have dispersed.
Ventilation and wind conditions affect where released gases can accumulate.
Hydrogen sulphide can rapidly overcome people and rescuers should not enter without a planned safe system.
Open stores and access points need secure barriers, covers or gates to prevent falls and unauthorised entry.
Emergency arrangements should address shutdown, communication, first aid and specialist rescue without creating additional casualties.
families.g: Slurry risk depends on store design, gas concentration, agitation, ventilation, weather, access control, machinery, work sequence and emergency capability.
